questions.q: State the two main phases in the life cycle of a plant and name the ploidy level of each phase.
questions.a: The two phases are the diploid (2n) sporophyte, which produces spores by meiosis, and the haploid (n) gametophyte, which produces gametes by mitosis. A wrong answer (e.g., saying both phases are diploid or confusing sporophyte with gametophyte) reveals the student has not grasped the core concept of alternation of generations and the ploidy shift that defines plant life cycles.

questions.q: A student argues that Cuscuta (dodder) and Venus flytrap should be moved out of Kingdom Plantae because they obtain nutrients from other organisms. Explain why this argument is incorrect using two defining features of Plantae.
questions.a: Cuscuta and Venus flytrap remain in Plantae because they possess eukaryotic cells with cellulose cell walls and chloroplasts (though reduced in Cuscuta), and they are fundamentally photosynthetic organisms that have evolved partial heterotrophy as an adaptation. A wrong answer that focuses only on nutrition mode shows the student treats heterotrophy as an exclusionary criterion, ignoring the primary phylogenetic characters (cell wall, pigment, ancestry) used in Whittaker's classification.

questions.q: Given an unknown green, eukaryotic, cellulose-walled organism that produces spores in a capsule atop a stalk and has a dominant, free-living gametophyte, predict its plant group and justify using two features.
questions.a: The organism is a bryophyte (moss). Reasoning: (1) Dominant, free-living gametophyte is characteristic of bryophytes; (2) Sporophyte is dependent and consists of a capsule on a stalk (seta) — unlike pteridophytes where sporophyte is dominant and independent. A wrong prediction (e.g., pteridophyte) indicates the student confuses the dominant generation and sporophyte structure across plant groups.

questions.q: Compare the cell wall composition of Kingdom Fungi and Kingdom Plantae. How does this difference support their separation into distinct kingdoms despite both being eukaryotic and having cell walls?
questions.a: Fungi have chitin (a nitrogen-containing polysaccharide) in their cell walls, while Plantae have cellulose (a glucose polymer). This biochemical difference reflects distinct evolutionary lineages and metabolic strategies: fungi are absorptive heterotrophs (saprophytes/parasites) with chitin providing structural rigidity for hyphal networks, whereas plants are photosynthetic autotrophs with cellulose suited for rigid, upright tissues. A student who only says "both have cell walls" misses the taxonomic significance of wall chemistry.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "All members of Kingdom Plantae are strictly autotrophic." Provide a counterexample and explain why the counterexample does not violate the kingdom's definition.
questions.a: The statement is false. Counterexamples: insectivorous plants (e.g., Bladderwort, Venus flytrap) and parasitic plants (e.g., Cuscuta). They are partially heterotrophic but retain eukaryotic cellulose-walled cells, chloroplasts (even if reduced), and embryonic development from a zygote — the defining synapomorphies of Plantae. A student who agrees with the statement holds a rigid, nutrition-only view of classification and fails to understand that kingdom boundaries are based on multiple phylogenetic characters.

questions.q: Design a simple observation-based activity using locally available plant material (e.g., moss, fern, flowering plant) to demonstrate the shift in dominant generation across three major plant groups. List the steps and the expected observation for each.
questions.a: Steps: (1) Collect a moss gametophyte (green carpet) and its sporophyte (stalked capsule). (2) Collect a fern sporophyte (frond) and locate the prothallus (gametophyte) in moist soil nearby. (3) Observe a flowering plant (e.g., mustard) — the visible plant is the sporophyte; the gametophyte is microscopic (pollen grain, embryo sac). Expected: Moss — gametophyte large, independent; sporophyte small, dependent. Fern — sporophyte large, independent; gametophyte small, free-living. Angiosperm — sporophyte dominant; gametophyte highly reduced, dependent. A poor answer that cannot distinguish the visible phases shows the student has not internalised the alternation of generations concept.
